status_reason: Glucose and viable biomass are defined targets, but fluorescence has no route to glucose, and the biomass route needs an independent viability reference plus process facts the client has not given. Fluorescence cannot be approved on sensitivity alone.
answer: Sensitivity alone does not justify fluorescence here: fluorimetry is rated high in sensitivity but low in selectivity, and most chemicals do not fluoresce. Glucose is not among the intrinsic fluorophores the sources list, so Raman or NIR, which the sources assign to glucose directly, are the methods to test. Viable biomass needs a defined signal and an independent viability reference before any fluorescence-based claim, so the first step is a laboratory study on your fermentation samples.

inline.headline: Test Raman on fermentation samples for glucose, with NIR as the comparison, before any in-line claim
inline.probe: Raman fiber probe with 785 nm excitation (as in the cited pharma study); report Raman shift in cm-1
inline.install: Not stated by the client; each method needs its own interface, so the probe position must be confirmed with the process
inline.fiber: Vis-NIR silica (350-2400 nm), Al/Cu-coated for Raman
inline.test_against: NIR reflection or transflection probe on the same samples
inline.not_final_because: No viable-cell reference, organism, medium, probe location or spectra were supplied, and the Raman glucose route has not been tested in this process.

problems.text: Sensitivity is not selectivity: fluorimetry is rated high in sensitivity but low in selectivity, and it relies on secondary emission from certain substances, since most chemicals do not fluoresce. The combined-probe study limits fluorescence to samples with at least one fluorescent component.
Glucose has no direct fluorescence route: the bioprocess material lists intrinsic fluorophores such as NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin for fluorescence, and assigns glucose to NIR and Raman.

Viable biomass needs a defined signal and an independent reference: the sources link optical signals to turbidity and cell density and describe no viable-cell measurement. NIR combined with fluorescence gave more accurate biomass in yeast fermentation, but a viability reference is still required.

methods.why: Gives direct detection of glucose in aqueous media; signals are weak and can be masked by fluorescence, so probe and filter design matter.
Tracks glucose in the millimolar range and is the most common online fiber-probe method, but may lack sensitivity below 0.1 %.
Not suitable for glucose; useful only for intrinsic fluorophores (NADH, tryptophan, riboflavin) and as a partner to NIR for biomass.
A low-cost biomass tool because turbidity correlates with cell density; it measures cell density, not viability, and the probe must match the optical density.

questions.q: Do you have an independent laboratory measurement of viable cells from the fermentation, and how often is it taken?
questions.why: Viable biomass cannot be reported without it; the sources link optical signals only to cell density.

questions.q: Which organism and medium are fermented, and is the broth clear, turbid or highly concentrated?
questions.why: Probe choice follows optical density, and the sources show different probes for transparent and opaque media.

questions.q: What glucose range and accuracy do you need, and what accuracy do you need for viable biomass?
questions.why: NIR may lack sensitivity below 0.1 %, so the target range decides whether NIR is adequate or Raman is needed.

questions.q: Where can a probe be placed in the process (vessel port, loop or bypass), and what access constraints apply?
questions.why: Each method needs its own interface, and the task decides the method and technique.

experiment.objective: Test whether Raman (glucose) and NIR, optionally with fluorescence, predict glucose and viable biomass against independent laboratory values in your fermentation.
steps: Sample one or more fermentation runs and take independent laboratory glucose and viable-cell values for each sample.
Record Raman spectra (785 nm excitation, Raman shift in cm-1) and NIR spectra of the same samples.
Record fluorescence spectra of the same samples to test whether any intrinsic fluorophore tracks biomass.
Build chemometric models on one set of samples and validate them on an independent set against the laboratory values.
Compare the NIR plus fluorescence fused model with the best single method on the same validation data.
experiment.go_no_go: Client sets the glucose and viable biomass accuracy targets; no-go if no model meets them on independent samples or if the combination does not beat the best single method.

pathway.key_features: Not yet identifiable: no spectra were supplied; glucose and biomass features must be selected from the laboratory spectra.
pathway.path_reason: The AFS pathway starts with a multi-method laboratory trial on the customer process before any model or system.

multispectral.why: NIR tracks major components such as glucose at millimolar levels, while fluorescence adds intrinsic fluorophores at high sensitivity, so the information is complementary; NIR plus fluorescence gave more accurate yeast biomass.
multispectral.test: Compare the fused model against the best single method (NIR alone, and Raman alone if tested) on the same independent validation samples with laboratory glucose and viable-cell references; keep the combination only if it wins.

assumptions: The broth is aqueous, so Raman is assumed suitable, since water absorbs weakly (S01-16-bio-raman).
The fermentation medium is treated as homogeneous, so separate synchronised probes are assumed; this must be checked.
Organism, medium, probe location and process volume are not stated and are treated as unknown.
